paragraphs: I have always noticed how commonly people lack the courage to share strange psychological experiences, even people of exceptional intelligence and culture. Almost everyone fears that whatever they might describe will find no parallel or response in the listener’s inner life, and might be doubted or laughed at. A truthful traveller who had seen an extraordinary creature resembling a sea serpent would not be afraid to mention it. Yet the same traveller would hesitate greatly before admitting to an unusual premonition, impulse, wandering thought, so-called vision, dream or other remarkable mental impression. I attribute much of the obscurity surrounding these subjects to that reluctance. We do not habitually share our experiences of these inward things as we share our experiences of the outside world. As a result, our collective experience of such matters seems exceptional—and truly is exceptional, in being so miserably incomplete.

In what I am about to describe, I have no intention of proposing, opposing or supporting any theory at all. I know the history of the Bookseller of Berlin. I have studied the case of the wife of a deceased Astronomer Royal, as told by Sir David Brewster. I have also followed the smallest details of a far more remarkable case of illusory apparitions within my own circle of friends. About this last case, I may need to state that the sufferer, a woman, was not related to me in any way, however distantly. A mistaken assumption about that might suggest an explanation for part of my own case—but only part—that would have no foundation at all. My experience cannot be attributed to an inherited peculiarity that had developed in me. I had never experienced anything at all like it before, and have never experienced anything at all like it since.

It does not matter how many years ago, or how few, a certain murder was committed in England and attracted great attention. We hear more than enough about murderers as they rise, one after another, to their dreadful fame. If I could, I would bury the memory of this particular brute as his body was buried in Newgate Jail. I deliberately give no direct clue to his identity.

When the murder was first discovered, no suspicion fell on the man who was later brought to trial. Or rather, since I cannot be too precise about my facts, no one publicly suggested that any suspicion fell on him. The newspapers did not mention him at that time, so they plainly could not have given any description of him then. It is essential to remember this fact.

At breakfast I unfolded my morning newspaper, which contained the account of that first discovery. I found it deeply interesting and read it closely, twice, if not three times. The discovery had been made in a bedroom. When I put the paper down, I was aware of a flash—a rush—a flow. I do not know what to call it; no word I can find describes it properly. In it, I seemed to see that bedroom passing through my room, like a picture impossibly painted on a running river. It passed almost instantly, but it was perfectly clear. So clear that, distinctly and with relief, I noticed there was no dead body on the bed.

I had this strange sensation in no romantic setting, but in rooms in Piccadilly, very close to the corner of St James’s Street. It was entirely new to me. At the time I was sitting in my armchair. A peculiar shiver accompanied the sensation and moved the chair from its place. It should be noted, however, that the chair rolled easily on castors. I went to one of the windows—there are two in the room, which is on the second floor—to refresh my eyes with the movement below in Piccadilly. It was a bright autumn morning, and the street sparkled cheerfully. A strong wind was blowing. As I looked out, it carried a mass of fallen leaves down from the Park. A gust caught them and spun them into a spiral column. As the column fell and the leaves scattered, I saw two men on the opposite side of the road, walking from west to east. One followed the other. The man in front kept looking back over his shoulder. The second followed about thirty paces behind, his right hand raised threateningly. First I noticed the strangeness and persistence of such a threatening gesture on a busy public street. Then I noticed something still more remarkable: no one paid any attention. Both men threaded their way among the other people with a smoothness hardly consistent even with walking on a pavement. So far as I could see, no one made way for them, touched them or looked after them. As they passed my windows, both stared up at me. I saw their faces very clearly and knew I could recognise them anywhere. I had not consciously noticed anything particularly remarkable about either face, except that the first man looked unusually grim and threatening, and the second man’s face was the colour of impure wax.

I am unmarried, and my personal servant and his wife are my entire household staff. I work at a certain branch bank. I wish my duties as head of a department were as light as people generally suppose. They kept me in town that autumn, when I needed a change. I was not ill, but I was not well. My reader may make as much as is reasonable of the fact that I felt worn out, was depressed by the monotony of my life, and had “slight indigestion.” My distinguished doctor assures me that my actual health at that time warrants no stronger description. I quote his own words from the written answer he gave when I asked him.

As the facts of the murder gradually emerged and increasingly occupied the public mind, I kept them out of mine. Amid the universal excitement, I learned as little as possible. But I knew that a verdict of Wilful Murder had been returned against the suspected murderer, and that he had been sent to Newgate to await trial. I also knew the trial had been postponed for one session of the Central Criminal Court because of widespread prejudice and insufficient time to prepare the defence. I may also have known when, or roughly when, the session to which the trial had been postponed would begin. But I believe I did not.

My sitting room, bedroom and dressing room are all on the same floor. The dressing room can be reached only through the bedroom. It does have a door that once opened onto the staircase, but part of my bath fittings is fixed across it, and had already been there for some years at that time. As part of the same alterations, the door had been nailed shut and covered with canvas.

Late one night I stood in my bedroom, giving my servant some instructions before he went to bed. I faced the only usable door into the dressing room. It was closed, and my servant had his back to it. While I spoke, I saw the door open and a man look in, beckoning to me with great urgency and mystery. He was the second of the two men who had walked along Piccadilly, the one whose face was the colour of impure wax.

After beckoning, the figure withdrew and closed the door. Without waiting longer than it took me to cross the bedroom, I opened the dressing-room door and looked inside. I already held a lighted candle. I had no inward expectation of finding the figure there, and I did not see it.

Aware that my servant stood astonished, I turned to him. “Derrick,” I said, “could you believe that, with all my senses clear, I thought I saw a—” At that point I laid my hand on his chest. He suddenly started, trembled violently and said, “Oh Lord, yes, sir! A dead man beckoning!”

Now I do not believe that John Derrick, my faithful, devoted servant for more than twenty years, had any impression of seeing such a figure until I touched him. The change in him at my touch was so startling that I firmly believe he received the impression from me, in some hidden, mysterious way, at that very instant.

I told John Derrick to bring some brandy. I gave him a small measure and was glad to take one myself. I told him nothing at all of what had happened before that night’s appearance. Thinking it over, I was absolutely certain I had never seen that face before except on the one occasion in Piccadilly. I compared its expression while beckoning in the doorway with its expression when it had stared up at me at the window. I concluded that, on the first occasion, it had tried to impress itself upon my memory, and on the second, it had made sure of being recognised at once.

I was not very comfortable that night, although I felt a certainty, difficult to explain, that the figure would not return. At daylight I fell into a heavy sleep. John Derrick woke me by coming to my bedside with a paper in his hand.

It seemed this paper had caused an argument at the door between the man delivering it and my servant. It was a summons to serve on a jury at the coming session of the Central Criminal Court at the Old Bailey. As John Derrick knew well, I had never been summoned to such a jury before. He believed—I am still unsure whether rightly or wrongly—that jurors of that kind were usually selected on a lower qualification than mine. At first he had refused to accept the summons. The man serving it had remained quite calm. He said my attendance or non-attendance meant nothing to him. There was the summons; I could deal with it at my own risk, not his.

For a day or two I could not decide whether to answer the summons or ignore it. I felt no mysterious preference, influence or attraction in either direction. I am as certain of that as of every other statement I make here. In the end I decided to go, as a break in the monotony of my life.

The appointed morning was cold and damp, in November. A dense brown fog filled Piccadilly. East of Temple Bar it became positively black and oppressively thick. The courthouse passages and stairs blazed with gaslight, and the court itself was lit in the same way. I think I did not know the Murderer was to be tried that day until officers led me into the crowded Old Court. I think that, until they got me inside with considerable difficulty, I did not know which of the two courts in session my summons would take me to. But do not take either statement as definite. I am not completely certain of either point.

I sat in the place reserved for waiting jurors and looked around the court as well as I could through its heavy cloud of fog and breath. I noticed the black vapour hanging like a murky curtain outside the great windows. I noticed the muffled sound of wheels on the straw or tanners’ bark scattered in the street, and the hum of the people gathered there. Now and then a shrill whistle, a louder song or a shout pierced that hum. Soon the two judges entered and took their seats. The buzz in the court fell into an awe-filled silence. An order was given to bring the Murderer into the dock. He appeared. At that instant, I recognised the first of the two men who had walked down Piccadilly.

If my name had been called then, I doubt I could have answered loudly enough to be heard. But it came around sixth or eighth on the list, and by then I could say, “Here!” Now, pay attention. As I stepped into the jury box, the prisoner, who had been watching closely without any sign of concern, became violently agitated and beckoned to his lawyer. His wish to object to my serving was so obvious that proceedings paused. With his hand on the dock, the lawyer whispered to his client and shook his head. Afterwards, the lawyer told me the prisoner’s first frightened words had been, “At any cost, object to that man serving!” But he would give no reason. He admitted he had not even known my name until he heard it called and saw me appear. So no objection was made.

I have already explained that I wish to avoid reviving the unhealthy memory of that Murderer. A detailed account of his long trial is also unnecessary to my story. I will therefore limit myself strictly to those incidents, during the ten days and nights we jurors were kept together, that directly concern my own strange experience. That is what I want to interest my reader in, rather than the Murderer. I ask you to attend to that, rather than to a page of the Newgate Calendar.

I was chosen as the jury’s foreman. On the second morning of the trial, after we had heard evidence for two hours—I heard the church clocks strike—I happened to look over my fellow jurors and found an inexplicable difficulty in counting them. I counted them several times, always with the same difficulty. In short, I counted one too many.

I touched the juror beside me and whispered, “Would you count us, please?” He seemed surprised, but turned his head and counted. “Why,” he said suddenly, “there are thirt— But no, that’s impossible. No. There are twelve of us.”

Whenever I counted that day, the individual numbers were right, but the total was always one too many. No apparition, no figure, accounted for it. But now I had an inward forewarning of the figure that was surely coming.

The jury stayed at the London Tavern. We all slept in one large room on separate tables. We were constantly in the care and under the eye of the officer sworn to keep us in his custody. I see no reason to conceal his real name. He was intelligent, extremely polite and helpful, and, I was glad to hear, highly respected in the City. He had a pleasant appearance, good eyes, enviable black whiskers and a fine, resonant voice. His name was Mr Harker.

When we went to our twelve beds at night, Mr Harker’s bed was pulled across the door. On the second night I did not feel like lying down. Seeing him sitting on his bed, I went to sit beside him and offered him a pinch of snuff. As he took it from my box, his hand touched mine. A peculiar shiver passed through him, and he said, “Who is this?”

I followed Mr Harker’s eyes along the room and again saw the figure I expected: the second of the two men who had walked down Piccadilly. I stood up, took a few steps, then stopped and looked back at Mr Harker. Quite unconcerned, he laughed and said pleasantly, “For a moment I thought we had a thirteenth juror without a bed. But I see it is the moonlight.”

I told Mr Harker nothing, but invited him to walk with me to the far end of the room. I watched the figure. It stood for a few moments beside the bed of each of my eleven fellow jurors, close to the pillow. It always went to the right-hand side of the bed, and always moved away across the foot of the next bed. From its head movements, it seemed merely to look down thoughtfully at each lying figure. It took no notice of me or my bed, which was nearest Mr Harker’s. It seemed to leave through a high window where the moonlight entered, as though by a flight of stairs in the air.
At breakfast the next morning, it emerged that everyone present except Mr Harker and me had dreamed of the murdered man during the night.

I now felt as certain that the second man who had walked down Piccadilly was the murdered man, so to speak, as if he had told me so himself. But even this happened, and in a way I was quite unprepared for.

On the fifth day of the trial, as the prosecution’s case drew to a close, a miniature portrait of the murdered man was presented as evidence. It had been missing from his bedroom when the crime was discovered, and later found in a hiding place where the Murderer had been seen digging. After the witness under examination identified it, it was handed up to the judges, then down for the jury to inspect. An officer in a black gown was bringing it towards me when the figure of the second man from Piccadilly burst from the crowd. It snatched the miniature from the officer and handed it to me with its own hands. Before I had seen the portrait, which was inside a locket, it said in a low, hollow voice, “I was younger then, and my face had not been drained of blood.” It also came between me and the juror to whom I was about to pass the miniature, then between him and the juror to whom he was about to give it. In this way, it passed the portrait through all of us and back to me. None of the others noticed.

From the first, we naturally discussed the day’s proceedings a great deal at meals, and whenever we were shut up together in Mr Harker’s care. On the fifth day, with the prosecution’s case complete before us, our discussion grew livelier and more serious. Among us was a member of a parish governing committee—the densest idiot I have ever seen at liberty. He met the plainest evidence with the most absurd objections. Two flabby parasites from the parish sided with him. All three had been selected from a district so given over to Fever that they themselves should have been on trial for five hundred Murders. Towards midnight, while some of us were already getting ready for bed and these troublesome blockheads were at their loudest, I saw the murdered man again. He stood grimly behind them, beckoning to me. As soon as I approached and joined the conversation, he withdrew. This began a separate series of appearances, all in the long room where we were confined. Whenever a group of my fellow jurors put their heads together, I saw the murdered man’s head among theirs. Whenever their comparison of notes went against him, he would beckon to me solemnly and irresistibly.

Remember that until the miniature was produced on the trial’s fifth day, I had never seen the Apparition in court. Now, as the defence began its case, three things changed. I will mention two of them together first. The figure was now constantly in court. There it never addressed me, but always whoever was speaking at the time. For example, the murdered man’s throat had been cut straight across. In the defence’s opening speech, it was suggested that he might have cut his own throat. At that very moment the figure stood at the speaker’s elbow, its throat in the dreadful state it had previously hidden. It gestured again and again across its windpipe, first with its right hand, then with its left, vigorously suggesting to the speaker that such a wound could not have been self-inflicted with either hand. In another example, a woman giving character evidence testified that the prisoner was the most pleasant of men. At that instant the figure stood on the floor in front of her, looking her full in the face. With its arm extended and finger outstretched, it pointed out the prisoner’s evil face.

The third change struck me powerfully as the most noticeable and remarkable of all. I offer no theory about it. I state it accurately and leave it there. Those the Apparition addressed did not see it, but whenever it approached them, they showed some fear or disturbance. It seemed to me that laws which did not apply to me prevented it from fully revealing itself to others. Yet it seemed able, invisibly, silently and darkly, to overshadow their minds. When the chief defence lawyer suggested suicide, the figure stood at his elbow, making a dreadful sawing motion across its severed throat. The lawyer undeniably faltered, lost the thread of his clever argument for a few seconds, wiped his forehead with his handkerchief, and turned extremely pale. When the Apparition confronted the character witness, her eyes most certainly followed its pointing finger and rested on the prisoner’s face with great hesitation and distress. Two more examples will be enough. On the eighth day of the trial, after the daily pause in the early afternoon for a few minutes’ rest and refreshment, I returned to court with the other jurors some time before the judges. Standing in the jury box and looking around, I thought the figure was absent. Then I happened to look up at the gallery and saw it bending forward over a very respectable woman, as if checking whether the judges had returned to their seats. Immediately afterwards she screamed, fainted and was carried out. It was the same with the venerable, wise and patient judge conducting the trial. When the case was over and he settled himself and his papers to sum up, the murdered man entered through the judges’ door. He approached the judge’s desk and looked eagerly over his shoulder at the pages of notes he was turning. The judge’s face changed. His hand stopped. The peculiar shiver I knew so well passed through him. He faltered, “Excuse me for a few moments, gentlemen. The stale air is making me feel rather unwell.” He recovered only after drinking a glass of water.

For six of those interminable ten days, everything was monotonously the same: the same judges and others on the bench; the same Murderer in the dock; the same lawyers at the table; the same tones of question and answer rising to the court’s roof; the same scratching of the judge’s pen; the same ushers coming and going; the same lights lit at the same hour whenever there had been natural daylight; the same foggy curtain outside the great windows when it was foggy; the same pattering and dripping rain when it was rainy; the same footprints of jailers and prisoner, day after day, on the same sawdust; the same keys locking and unlocking the same heavy doors. Through all that weary monotony, which made me feel I had been the jury’s foreman for an immense stretch of time and that Piccadilly had flourished at the same time as Babylon, the murdered man never became the least bit less distinct to my eyes. At no time was he less clear than anyone else. I must not omit this fact: I never once saw the Apparition I call the murdered man look at the Murderer. Again and again I wondered, “Why doesn’t he?” But he never did.

Nor did he look at me after the miniature was produced, until the trial’s final moments. We withdrew to consider our verdict at seven minutes before ten at night. The idiotic parish official and his two parish parasites caused so much trouble that we twice returned to court to ask for certain passages from the judge’s notes to be read again. Nine of us had not the slightest doubt about them, and I believe no one else in court did either. The three blockheads had no purpose but obstruction, and disputed the passages for that very reason. At last we prevailed. The jury finally returned to court at ten minutes past twelve.

The murdered man stood directly opposite the jury box, across the court. As I took my place, he looked at me very attentively. He seemed satisfied. For the first time, he carried a great grey veil on his arm. Slowly he shook it out over his head and his whole body. As I delivered our verdict, “Guilty,” the veil collapsed. Everything vanished, and the place where he had stood was empty.

As was customary, the judge asked the Murderer whether he had anything to say before the death sentence was passed. He muttered something indistinctly. The next day’s leading newspapers described it as “a few rambling, incoherent and barely audible words, in which he was understood to complain that he had not had a fair trial because the jury’s foreman was prejudiced against him.” What he actually said was this remarkable declaration: “My Lord, I knew I was a doomed man when the foreman of my jury entered the box. My Lord, I knew he would never let me off. Before I was arrested, he somehow came to my bedside in the night, woke me and put a rope around my neck.”
